findings: No sustained arrhythmia. No pauses greater than 2 seconds. No AV block.

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No haemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or large-territory infarct.

findings: Structurally normal heart. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion.

alternatives: Candesartan 8-16 mg daily (also lowers blood pressure) if propranolol is not tolerated, with reliable contraception.
Metoprolol 100-200 mg daily as an alternative beta-blocker.
contraindications: Propranolol: asthma or bronchospasm, second- or third-degree AV block, sinus bradycardia, decompensated heart failure, severe peripheral arterial disease.
Sumatriptan: uncontrolled hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, previous stroke or TIA, peripheral vascular disease; within 24 h of an ergot or another triptan.
Candesartan: pregnancy (fetotoxic in the second and third trimesters).
output.formulary_status: Propranolol 40 mg tablets and 80 mg modified-release capsules, candesartan 4 mg and 8 mg tablets and sumatriptan 50 mg and 100 mg tablets on formulary.
interactions: Propranolol with sumatriptan: no clinically relevant pharmacokinetic interaction; no sumatriptan dose change. (Propranolol raises rizatriptan exposure by about 70%, so rizatriptan is limited to 5 mg; this does not apply to sumatriptan.)
Propranolol with alcohol: additive blood-pressure lowering; no clinically important interaction at social intake.
output.proposed: Propranolol for migraine prevention, with sumatriptan 50 mg as needed
output.summary: No interaction between propranolol and sumatriptan; the propranolol dose limit applies to rizatriptan only. Sources: propranolol, sumatriptan, rizatriptan and candesartan SmPC; Silberstein SD et al., Neurology 2012;78:1337-1345.
warnings: Propranolol: fatigue, reduced exercise tolerance, vivid dreams, depression; may mask hypoglycaemia; do not stop abruptly.
Propranolol in pregnancy: fetal growth restriction and neonatal bradycardia or hypoglycaemia are reported; use only if needed, with monitoring.
Sumatriptan: check blood pressure periodically; take at headache onset, not during the aura.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Stereotyped visual aura over 20-30 min followed by headache, 5 of 6 criterion C characteristics; 2-3 severely disabling days a month; no red flag; BP controlled
action_criteria.label: Take a structured headache and aura history with neurological examination and red-flag review, applying every ICHD-3 1.2 criterion explicitly
action_criteria.rationale: Migraine with typical aura is a clinical diagnosis (ICHD-3 1.2.1); the history also quantifies disability for the preventive decision and screens for the red flags that would justify imaging (AAN 2000).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Adding the beta-blocker needs no change to her triptan dose; the triptan stays allowed while blood pressure is controlled
action_criteria.label: Optionally check the proposed preventive against her sumatriptan and blood pressure
action_criteria.rationale: No real interaction exists between propranolol and sumatriptan and her hypertension is controlled, so the check does not change management. Sources: propranolol and sumatriptan SmPC.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on preventive treatment of migraine in patients with hypertension
action_criteria.label: Optionally consult the literature on migraine prevention with comorbid hypertension
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading only; not a clinical step in the patient's pathway.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not continue or start combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch or ring): migraine with aura is UKMEC category 4; offer a progestogen-only method or an IUD.
Do not attribute the attacks to her hypertension: stage 1 hypertension does not cause a stereotyped visual aura.
Do not withdraw sumatriptan because of her controlled stage 1 hypertension: triptans are contraindicated only when hypertension is uncontrolled.
Do not prescribe codeine-containing analgesics (documented intolerance).
required_recommendations: Make the diagnosis of migraine with typical visual aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1) on clinical grounds: no red flag is present, so no neuroimaging is needed.

Offer preventive treatment for 2-3 severely disabling headache days a month, rising over 6 months (AHS 2021: consider at 2, offer at 3 or more): propranolol, starting 40 mg twice daily or 80 mg modified-release daily and titrating to 80-160 mg a day, after checking for asthma, bradycardia or heart block and depression; it also lowers blood pressure [Silberstein_2012]. Candesartan is the alternative only with reliable contraception.

Continue sumatriptan at headache onset (not during the aura), up to 100 mg per dose if 50 mg is insufficient, with an antiemetic (metoclopramide 10 mg or domperidone 10 mg) for vomiting; no dose change is needed with propranolol.
Continue lifestyle management of her stage 1 hypertension with periodic blood pressure checks; triptans become contraindicated if hypertension is uncontrolled.
Address triggers: regular sleep within her shift pattern where possible and reduced alcohol; keep a headache diary to judge the preventive response at 2-3 months.
Advise that combined hormonal contraception (pill, patch or ring) is UKMEC category 4 in migraine with aura; if contraception is wanted, offer a progestogen-only method or an IUD.

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve it for suspected subarachnoid haemorrhage with a normal CT or for meningitis, neither of which is present here.
Routine transthoracic or bubble echocardiography (PFO screening) is not indicated in migraine with aura; PFO closure did not meet its migraine end points in the MIST, PRIMA and PREMIUM trials.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; it has a role only when cardioembolic stroke is in question.

accepted: Migraine with typical visual aura (ICHD-3 1.2.1) with comorbid stage 1 hypertension

differential.diagnosis: Migraine without aura with rising frequency
differential.key_features: A stereotyped, well-documented visual aura precedes every headache: this is migraine with aura.
BP 128/78 mmHg today; hypertension-attributed headache needs a hypertensive crisis (180/120 mmHg or more) and does not produce a stereotyped aura; the attacks began 6 years before the hypertension.
PRES presents with acute severe hypertension, encephalopathy, seizures or visual loss; none present, BP 128/78 mmHg and normal examination.
Aura duration and stereotyped pattern over 7 years are inconsistent with seizure

key_clinical_evidence: Comorbid stage 1 hypertension does not change the migraine diagnosis but informs preventive selection (propranolol or candesartan also lower blood pressure)
Sumatriptan is not contraindicated in controlled stage 1 hypertension; blood pressure needs periodic review
2-3 severely disabling headache days a month meet the AHS 2021 criteria for preventive treatment (consider at 2, offer at 3 or more)
Shift-work sleep disruption is a modifiable trigger plausibly driving the recent frequency increase

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Stage 1 hypertension is comorbid; it began years after the aura and does not cause a stereotyped visual aura; it informs the preventive choice, not the diagnosis
red_herrings.intended_effect: May anchor on hypertensive headache, PRES or hypertensive visual symptoms

findings.result: Stereotyped attacks for 7 years; 1-2 a month rising to 2-3 a month over the past 6 months.
Visual only: bright paracentral spot expanding into multicoloured fortification spectra in one hemifield (either side), leaving a transient scotoma. No sensory, speech, motor or brainstem symptoms.
Gradual expansion over 20-30 min; fully reversible.
Throbbing headache, usually left-sided, 8/10, as the aura fades, with nausea, vomiting, photophobia and phonophobia; lasts 6-10 h; unable to function. 2-3 severely disabling headache days a month.
Sleep disruption from double shifts, wine, intense exertion. Sumatriptan 50 mg effective if taken early in the headache, about twice a month. Codeine intolerance (nausea and vomiting).
Stage 1 hypertension diagnosed last year, on lifestyle measures; BP 128/78 mmHg today.
Headache-free. Normal cranial nerves, visual fields and fundi (no papilloedema); normal power, reflexes, sensation, coordination and gait.

Systemic symptoms or fever: absent. Neoplasia history: absent. Neurological deficit between attacks: absent. Sudden onset: absent. Onset after 50: absent (onset at 28). Pattern change: frequency increase with shift work, aura and headache character unchanged. Positional or Valsalva trigger: absent. Papilloedema: absent. Pregnancy: not reported. Aura always on the same side: absent. No red flag present.

clinical_assessment.impression: Recurrent fully reversible visual aura with gradual spread over 20-30 min, followed by headache: meets ICHD-3 1.2.1.1 typical aura with headache (criterion C 5 of 6). 2-3 severely disabling headache days a month. No red flag; normal examination; BP 128/78 mmHg.

patient.chief_complaint: Visual zigzag followed by severe headache — now with 2-3 episodes per month

family_history: Mother had migraines throughout her 30s and 40s; father had hypertension; no stroke or coagulopathy history

social_history.note: Registered nurse; single; non-smoker; social alcohol; no illicit drugs; active (exercises when not working double shifts)

patient.history_present_illness:
A 35-year-old Black woman presented to the neurology outpatient clinic with a 7-year history of recurrent visual aura followed by severe headaches that have increased in frequency over the past 6 months from 1-2 to 2-3 per month. Each episode begins with a small bright spot in her central vision that gradually expands into a multicolored zigzag pattern (fortification spectra) spreading outward into one side of her vision (either side) over 20-30 minutes, leaving a temporary blind area. As the visual aura fades, she develops a severe throbbing headache, usually left-sided (8/10), with nausea, vomiting, photophobia, and phonophobia that lasts 6-10 hours. She often needs to go to a dark room and cannot function during episodes.

She reports that sumatriptan 50 mg (prescribed by her PCP 2 years ago) is effective when taken early in the headache phase but stops working if she delays treatment. She takes it approximately twice per month. She identifies sleep disruption, wine, and intense physical exertion as personal triggers. She is a nurse and has been working double shifts frequently due to understaffing, which correlates with the increased frequency. She is not on hormonal contraception. She has stage 1 hypertension, diagnosed by her PCP last year and managed with lifestyle modification (BP 128/78 today), and no other medical history. She denies any weakness, speech difficulty, or any episode characteristics that differ from her usual pattern.
